progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: An alphabetical psalm with a hole in it. After the superscription, each verse opens with the next letter of the alphabet, alef through tav, except that no verse begins with vav: the he verse is followed directly by the zayin verse. Then, after the tav verse has closed the sequence, one more verse is added, and it begins with pe, a letter already used earlier. The same two features appear in Psalm 25. The content is a testimony that turns into a lesson: the first half reports a rescue, the second half teaches a class of children how to live. Verse 4 is sung when the Torah scroll is lifted and carried, verse 11 is among the verses appended to the grace after meals, and in many rites the whole psalm is read in the morning service on Shabbat.

stichs.en: Of David.
When he changed his behaviour in front of Abimelech,
who drove him out, and he left.

verses.summary: The heading places the psalm at the lowest point of David's flight, when he saved himself by acting like a madman. The rescue the psalm celebrates was not a battle won.

stichs.en: I will bless the LORD at every moment;
His praise is always in my mouth.

verses.summary: The alef verse, and the first of the acrostic proper. The claim is about frequency, not intensity: at every time, continually, which is the promise the rest of the psalm has to make good on.

stichs.en: My soul boasts in the LORD;
the lowly hear it and are glad.

verses.summary: Boasting is normally the opposite of humility, so the second line answers the objection before it is raised: this boast is the one that the humble are pleased to overhear.

stichs.en: Make the LORD great with me,
and let us lift His name high together.

verses.summary: Two plural verbs, an imperative and a cohortative, turn a private testimony into a congregation. This is the verse the leader calls out when the scroll is carried to the reading desk.

stichs.en: I sought out the LORD and He answered me,
and He pulled me clear of everything I dreaded.

verses.summary: The first report in the past tense, and the pattern the psalm will repeat twice more: someone calls, He hears, He extracts. The noun is fears, not enemies, so what is removed is the dread rather than the danger.

stichs.en: They looked to Him and were lit up,
and their faces will never be shamed.

verses.summary: The he verse, and the last before the gap in the alphabet. Note the change of mood inside it: the first half reports what happened, the second half is a wish, marked by the negative particle that goes with a jussive.

stichs.en: This poor man called and the LORD heard,
and saved him out of all his troubles.

verses.summary: The zayin verse, arriving where a vav verse would be expected. The demonstrative points at someone: either the speaker calling himself poor, or a case held up in front of the listeners.

stichs.en: The messenger of the LORD camps around those who fear Him,
and He pulls them free.

verses.summary: One participle and one finite verb: a camp that stays put and a rescue that happens. The military image is defensive, a ring of guard around the people who are afraid.

stichs.en: Taste and see that the LORD is good;
happy is the man who shelters in Him.

verses.summary: The argument stops being reported and becomes an invitation. Tasting comes before seeing, which is the wrong order for a proof and the right one for an experience.

stichs.en: Fear the LORD, you His holy ones,
for those who fear Him lack nothing.

verses.summary: Fear here is not the opposite of the radiance in verse 6; the same participle for those who fear Him appears in verse 8 as the ones the camp protects. What it buys is stated flatly: no shortage.

stichs.en: Young lions go poor and go hungry,
but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.

verses.summary: The strongest hunter in the field is set against the one who has nothing but a search. The verb for lacking is the same root as the noun in verse 10. This verse is said at the end of the grace after meals.

stichs.en: Come, sons, listen to me;
the fear of the LORD I will teach you.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. Testimony becomes instruction, and the vocabulary switches to the wisdom-book register of a teacher addressing students as sons.

stichs.en: Who is the man who wants life,
who loves days enough to see good in them?

verses.summary: A question addressed to the market rather than the study house, phrased the way a seller would phrase it. The answer given next has nothing to do with health or wealth.

stichs.en: Guard your tongue from evil,
and your lips from speaking deceit.

verses.summary: The whole answer to the question is a rule about speech. These words open the silent meditation that closes every standing prayer, which is why most learners meet this verse before they meet the psalm.

stichs.en: Turn from evil and do good;
seek peace and chase it down.

verses.summary: Four imperatives, two negative and two positive. The last one raises the temperature: peace is not waited for but pursued, with the verb used for hunting a fugitive.

stichs.en: The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous,
and His ears toward their cry for help.

verses.summary: The ayin verse, and the start of a run of three that describe God by body parts: eyes, ears, then face. Attention is the reward, stated before any rescue is mentioned.

stichs.en: The face of the LORD is set against those who do evil,
to cut their memory off from the earth.

verses.summary: The pe verse, in its regular alphabetical place. The same face that shines in verse 6 is turned the other way here, and the punishment named is erasure from memory rather than death.

stichs.en: They cried out and the LORD heard,
and rescued them from all their troubles.

verses.summary: Verse 7 repeated in the plural: the one poor man has become a group, and the singular suffixes on troubles and saved him turn into plural ones.

stichs.en: The LORD is close to the broken of heart,
and He saves those crushed in spirit.

verses.summary: Two construct chains describing damaged people, and a single adjective, near, doing the work. Nothing is said about repairing them first.

stichs.en: Many are the troubles of a righteous man,
and out of them all the LORD delivers him.

verses.summary: The concession the psalm has been circling: being righteous does not reduce the number of troubles. It changes only what happens at the end of each one.

stichs.en: He guards every one of his bones;
not one of them has been broken.

verses.summary: The claim narrows from troubles to bones, the hardest and most countable part of a body. The verb for breaking is the same root as the broken heart of verse 19, used there of what God draws near to and here of what He prevents.

stichs.en: Evil kills the wicked,
and those who hate the righteous will bear their guilt.

verses.summary: The tav verse, which should be the last one. Evil is the subject and the wicked the object, so the punishment is not sent from outside: it is the thing itself doing the killing.

stichs.en: The LORD ransoms the life of His servants,
and none who shelter in Him will bear guilt.

verses.summary: An extra verse after the alphabet has finished, opening with pe. It takes the verb that ended verse 22 and negates it, so the psalm closes on the acquittal of the other side rather than on the guilt of the wicked.

pardes.body: Two halves joined at verse 12. Verses 2 to 11 are a report: I sought, He answered, this poor man called, He heard, so taste for yourselves. Verses 12 to 23 are a lesson: come and listen, here is what to do with your tongue, and here is what happens to the two kinds of people. The alphabet runs underneath both halves and does not quite hold. Twenty-two verses follow the superscription, but they carry only twenty-one letters, alef through tav with no vav verse, and then a twenty-second verse that starts again with pe. The one place a vav does stand at the head of a line is inside the he verse, at {{6.3}}, where the second half of the couplet begins with it. Whether that is why the letter has no verse of its own, the text does not say.

The superscription and the turn of the psalm share a root. In {{1.3}} David changes his good sense, the noun for taste and judgement, in order to look insane in front of a foreign king; in {{9.0}} the same root comes back as an imperative addressed to everyone, taste. The word that named a pretended madness names the recommended way to know that God is good. A second pairing closes the poem: the verb at {{22.5}}, they will bear guilt, is the last word of the tav verse, and the added pe verse repeats it at {{23.5}} with a negative in front. Note also that the psalm has both an ayin verse at {{16.0}} and a pe verse at {{17.0}} in their normal order, so the extra pe at {{23.0}} is a genuine addition rather than a displaced letter.

Verses 13 and 14 became the classic text on guarding speech. The Talmud tells of a peddler who went through the towns crying that he had the elixir of life for sale; when a crowd gathered he opened a book of Psalms and read out the question, who is the man who wants life, together with its answer, guard your tongue from evil. Those same words of {{7.1}} onward, the poor man who called and was heard, were read as the reason David could be quoted at all: the teacher of the second half is the rescued man of the first, and he is selling what he was given. The verse about bones at {{21.2}}, that not one is broken, was heard against the rule that no bone of the passover offering may be broken, so that the protected righteous stands where the offering stands.

The mystical readings work on the order of the two verbs in verse 9. Sight keeps its object at a distance and leaves the one seeing unchanged; taste takes the thing in and changes the one tasting, and it cannot be done on someone else's report. Putting taste first makes knowledge of God a matter of ingestion rather than observation, and the invitation is then unanswerable by argument. The missing letter is read in the same key. An alphabet is the full set of what can be said, and this one is short by a letter and long by a verse, so the psalm neither closes on completeness nor claims it: what falls outside the sequence is the verse that says nobody who shelters there is condemned.
